conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m the surgery doctor taking care of you. I understand you had a gastric bypass a few months ago and now you’re having upper belly pain. Can you tell me what’s been going on since yesterday?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It started yesterday—this burning pain right in the middle, like under my ribs. I felt nauseous and threw up once.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Was the vomit bloody or green? And have you been able to pass gas or have bowel movements?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No blood, not green—just food. I’m still passing gas. I’ve actually had more bowel movements than usual—like three loose ones.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any fever, chills, chest pain, shortness of breath, or trouble urinating?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No. Just the pain and nausea. I’m scared something is wrong with the bypass.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s completely understandable. Your vitals look stable and your belly exam is soft without guarding, which is reassuring. We’re going to check labs and get a CT scan with contrast to look at the bypass connections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is a CT safe after surgery? And what are you looking for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—this is a common test. We’re looking for things like a blockage, a leak, or irritation/ulcer near the connection. The contrast helps us see where fluid is traveling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. The pain is pretty bad right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll treat your pain with IV medication and also give nausea medicine. We’ll keep you from eating or drinking until we know more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do my blood tests show anything serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: So far your labs are reassuring—your white blood cell count is normal and your kidney function looks fine. Nothing suggests a major infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve lost about 50 pounds since the bypass. Could that be causing this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The weight loss itself isn’t the problem, but after bypass some people can develop irritation or ulcers near the gastrojejunal connection, which can cause this kind of pain and nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried about a blockage. Wouldn’t I be throwing up more?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Often with a blockage you’d have persistent vomiting and trouble passing gas. You’re still passing gas, which is a good sign, but we’ll let the imaging guide us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: They took blood for something called H. pylori. What is that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a bacteria that can contribute to ulcers. We’re checking a blood test for it. If it’s positive, we treat it with antibiotics; if it’s negative, we focus on acid suppression and other ulcer prevention.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When will I know the CT results?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We should have the read soon. Once we do, we’ll decide if you need an endoscopy to look directly at the connection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your CT is back. It does not show an obstruction. It does show contrast in both the small gastric pouch and the larger gastric remnant, which can suggest a possible communication between them. There’s also some dilation of the proximal efferent limb, but again no clear blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A communication—does that mean a hole? Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It suggests there may be a connection between the pouch and the remnant. The CT can’t always confirm exactly what it is. The good news is there’s no free air or fluid and no obstruction. To better understand what’s causing your pain, we’re planning an upper endoscopy today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What happens during the endoscopy? Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get sedation so you’re comfortable. A flexible camera goes through the mouth into the pouch and down to the connection. We can look for ulcers or narrowing and see if there’s bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could this be from reflux? I’ve had reflux before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Reflux can contribute to irritation, but after bypass, pain like this is often from an ulcer near the gastrojejunal anastomosis. Either way, acid suppression is a key part of treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We just finished the endoscopy. The gastric pouch looked unremarkable, and the connection to the small bowel was widely open. We saw two ulcers on the jejunal side within about 2 cm of the connection—one small superficial clean-based ulcer and one larger deeper cratered ulcer with a pigmented spot. There was no active bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s ulcers. Is that why it hurts so much?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—ulcers in that area can cause significant epigastric pain and nausea. The reassuring part is there’s no active bleeding and the connection is open.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What do we do to treat them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting a proton pump inhibitor—Protonix—through the IV once daily while you’re here to reduce acid and help healing. We’ll also control pain with IV morphine for now and then switch to oral medication when you’re tolerating intake.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Does this mean my bypass failed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. Ulcers can happen after bypass even when the surgery is otherwise intact. Your pouch and the connection looked good on endoscopy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I drink anything yet? My mouth is so dry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start slowly. Once your nausea is controlled and you’re awake from sedation, we’ll begin with a bariatric diet progression—starting with a Bariatric Stage 2 plan as tolerated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The morphine helps, but I don’t want to be on it long.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good goal. As soon as you’re taking liquids and your pain is improving, we’ll switch to an oral pain medication like a liquid oxycodone-acetaminophen solution.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How was the night—pain, nausea, and the loose stools?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Pain is better than yesterday. I still feel a little queasy. I had another loose stool overnight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Today we’ll keep you on Bariatric Stage 2 and transition your pain control from IV to oral liquid medication. We’ll keep the acid medicine going.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will the ulcer bleed? That pigmented spot sounds scary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: A pigmented spot can be a sign of a recent small bleed, but there was no active bleeding during the procedure. We’ll monitor your symptoms and blood counts, and the PPI helps reduce bleeding risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When will the H. pylori test come back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It should be back soon. If it’s negative, we won’t need antibiotics for that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your H. pylori blood test is negative.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what caused the ulcers then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sometimes ulcers occur from acid exposure at the connection site after bypass. The key is consistent acid suppression. We’ll send you home on a proton pump inhibitor twice a day, and it needs to be crushed so it absorbs properly after bypass.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous about eating. What if food makes it worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll advance slowly and stick to the bariatric diet stages. Small, frequent, appropriate foods and avoiding irritants will help. If pain spikes with intake, tell us right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you feeling today? Any vomiting or worsening pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting. Pain is much better. I did have some loose stools late last night though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. We can adjust your diet to see if that helps. Today we’ll advance you to Bariatric Stage III as long as you tolerate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Stage III is okay so far, but the diarrhea is annoying. Is it from the meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be from diet changes after bypass, and sometimes lactose can trigger it. If it continues, we can try a lactose-free approach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: This morning, since you’re still having loose stools, we’re switching you to a lactose-free diet. Also, we’ll switch your Protonix from IV to an oral form since you’re tolerating intake.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: If I’m going home, what medicine am I taking for the ulcers?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll take omeprazole 20 mg twice a day, and you should crush it before taking it. That’s the main ulcer-healing medication.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And for pain? I don’t want to overdo it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll have a liquid oxycodone-acetaminophen medication to use only as needed. The goal is to use the smallest amount necessary and taper off as your pain improves.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been anxious since this started. I keep thinking something will rupture.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. Based on the CT and endoscopy, we did not see obstruction or active bleeding, and your exam has stayed stable. We can also give you a small dose of alprazolam as needed for anxiety, but we’ll use it carefully, especially with any pain medicine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about that possible connection the CT mentioned between the pouch and remnant—do I need surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right now, we’re treating what we directly saw causing symptoms—the ulcers. The CT suggested a possible communication, but the immediate plan is medical treatment and close follow-up. If symptoms persist or worsen, your surgical team may recommend additional testing as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When can I go back to work?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can return to work as long as your pain is controlled without narcotic medications like oxycodone. If you still need them, it’s safer to wait.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Before discharge: you’re walking independently, tolerating oral intake and meds, and your pain is controlled on oral medication. We’ll send you home on crushed omeprazole twice daily, the liquid pain medication as needed, and alprazolam as needed for anxiety.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should make me come back to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Come back for worsening severe abdominal pain, repeated vomiting, vomiting blood, black stools, fever or chills, inability to keep liquids down, or feeling faint. Otherwise, follow up with your surgical team as arranged and stay on the bariatric diet plan, lactose-free if it helps the diarrhea.
